articles.title: Show HN: A language model that lives in a boot sector
articles.summary:
All the ideas came from the boot sector demo scene where people had been writing chess and BASIC games in 512 bytes, even a C compiler. I wondered what one can do using a neural network instead of a program and generating boot logs for non-existent hardware was something fun to try.
Entire inference engine is 510 bytes of MBR, weights, vocab, and strings reside in the sectors following MBR. Small char-level neural network was trained on dmesg generated by machine, so machine produces Linux boot messages infinitely.
train.py performs precisely the same integer arithmetic operations as the asm code does and thus produces an output identical character-by-character to the one produced by QEMU. The difference analysis revealed my favorite bug. The characters at the beginning matched those generated by the simulator, but then the output diverged. I retrieved the hidden layer via QEMU’s debug port and compared the neurons' values with those of the simulator, one neuron at a time. Only the value of the first neuron was correct. The activation involves idiv, and idiv stores its remainder in edx. The pointer to the biases table was stored in edx, which resulted in the first neuron being biased correctly and the following ones using garbage. Now the bias' address is determined from the loop counter, and no pointers have to survive the division. Another bug I found simply by looking at the code before I did my first run-through: the BIOS print routine zeros out bx, but bx contains the predicted character number. This explains the push and pop of bx surrounding the print.
sectorllm is the most similar to my project, as it runs an actual 5-layer llama2 with attention mechanism in just 1.2K of assembly code. It is the trade-off in the opposite direction, as my engine needs to fit into one sector and therefore my network has just one hidden layer of int8 operations for dreaming the dmesg.

articles.title: This Week in Package Management: 31 October 2026
articles.summary:
This week’s package management news, gathered from the package manager OPML feed collection, my posts and boosts on Mastodon, and anything people sent me.
Security
The Go blog’s eMudhra post-incident writeup covers Go’s first URGENT-track security release: Mozilla added eight eMudhra intermediates to OneCRL on 17 October, the Go security team was alerted on 19 October, and Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 shipped under seven and a half hours later with a patch that rejects any chain through those intermediates. The post also says Go plans to add revocation checking on Linux. A test page shows the git, curl and python3 that Apple ships with macOS still trusted the eMudhra intermediates on 28 October, and macOS 27.2 undid the workaround users had applied by hand.
sbt 1.13.1 and 2.0.12 fix a zip slip in IO.unzip and its variants (GHSA-p8jf-532w-4p65) that an earlier fix missed. pipx 1.18.7 now requires pip 26.2.2 or later in its shared libraries and replaces an older shared pip on the next pipx command instead of waiting for the 30-day refresh.
Releases
Composer 2.11 adds a cooldown dependency policy that withholds newly published versions for a configured period during update and require, with a --no-cooldown flag for installing a security fix straight away. It also removes the source fallback deprecated in 2.10 and lets custom policies block during composer install. 2.11.1 fixes GitLab CI job tokens against GitLab’s Composer registry.
pnpm 12.16 adds a global --env-file flag and fixes two security issues, one in zstd decompression and one in signing. 12.17 adds pnpm peers check --global and dependency-group selectors and wildcards in overrides, and pnpm outdated and pnpm update now cover runtime and package manager versions plus Cargo and Python dependencies. 11.28.9 fixes a crash on registry responses with too many content encodings (GHSA-xjj6-f33q-929c) and sizes the install worker pool from the container’s CPU quota.
Homebrew 7.0.11 verifies formula patch downloads from the API and requires verifiable sources for official formulae.
mise 2026.10.21 to 2026.10.25 adds mise bootstrap --config-dir so mise’s global config can be kept in a dotfiles checkout, deploys Stow-style packages without a per-package table, and lets mise bootstrap packages prune --force remove casks it cannot prove are unchanged.
Hatch 1.18.2 and Hatchling 1.33.0 support Python 3.15. Hatch’s managed 3.15 distributions are now the final 3.15.0 release, and the default test matrix includes 3.15 and the free-threaded 3.15t.
ORAS 1.3.6 narrows the bearer-realm denylist that 1.3.5 introduced. 1.3.5 rejected realms on any private address, which broke self-hosted split-host registries such as GitLab. The default now blocks only loopback, link-local, unspecified and cloud metadata addresses.
Harbor 2.16.0-rc1 replaces Redis with Valkey as the cache backend and builds for amd64 and arm64. It also proxies the referrers API to the upstream registry with paging and local merge.
Conan 2.34.0 makes a third fewer local cache database calls on installs from cache, sends original URLs to backup source remotes in an X-Conan-Origin-Urls header, and adds a command_alias.conf file for command shortcuts.
Gradle 9.9.0 RC1 keeps wrapper settings when upgrading the wrapper, filters non-method JUnit Platform tests, and compiles Kotlin DSL scripts faster.
Debcraft 1.0 (Otto Kekäläinen) builds Debian packages in a Podman or Docker container made from the suite in debian/changelog and the build dependencies in debian/control. It diffs the artifacts between two builds and automates importing new upstream versions.
Renovate 44.189.0 applies vulnerability alerts to transitive dependencies, opening security updates that change only the lockfile. 44.194.0 adds a manager for Paket, the .NET dependency manager. 44.184.0 reports gh actions-lock findings when the command fails and re-pins only the updated refs in actions.lock.
Also out:
RubyGems 4.1.0.beta3
uv 0.13.6
setup-uv 10.3.3
PDM 2.29.5
sbt 2.1.0-RC2
APT 3.3.5
Chocolatey 2.7.5 and 1.4.8
PSResourceGet 1.3.0-rc2
vcpkg tool 2026-10-29
vlt 1.6.1
Verdaccio 7.0.2
EasyBuild 5.4.2
Podman 6.2.0-rc1
Terraform 1.17.1
OpenTofu 1.13.5
Dependabot Core 0.402.0
Articles
tar-codec (William Woodruff, Astral) is a new Rust tar library and uv’s default tar reader as of 0.13. It is roughly twice as fast as the previous reader and reduces the risk of parser differentials: it refuses archives whose headers mix tar families, allows at most one GNU long-name and one long-link record per member, and refuses pax tombstones. UV_LEGACY_TAR_BACKEND=1 restores the old reader.
A consistent(-ish) npm dependency graph (Evert Pot, vlt) finds that 22% of new npm versions in a 24-hour window arrived with at least one dependency still missing from the registry. vlt’s npm replication now holds a publish until its transitive dependencies are also available, and releases anything still held after an hour.
PyPI now limits versions to 128 characters. Two of the roughly 9.9 million releases on PyPI have a version that long, half have five characters or fewer, and 99% have twenty or fewer. Projects owned by a PyPI organisation now get higher default limits: 200 MB per file instead of 100 MB, 20 GB per project instead of 10 GB, and ten new projects per day.
How to fund Rust contributors (Jakub Beránek, Rust Blog) sets out three routes: the Rust Foundation Maintainers Fund or RustNL Maintainers Team for general maintenance, fundable Rust Project Goals for specific features, and GitHub Sponsors for individual contributors.
Ruby Central’s OSS Changelog is back after a long gap. RubyGems.org now validates gem pushes against a schema built from the metadata of all 180,000+ published gems, and it revoked every legacy API key after a report that its CDN could cache that endpoint’s responses and serve them to the wrong user. The Gem Security team has scanned about 317 of 619 heavily downloaded gems with AI models. Reviewers rejected 120 of 134 findings, and one that survived was a critical password check bug in rubyntlm, fixed in 0.6.6.
Thirteen backlogs in a trenchcoat (Jamie Tanna) sorts Renovate’s open backlog of 1,688 ideas, 1,005 issues and 465 human-authored PRs into 13 buckets of work. Renovate’s own bot opened 59% of the project’s pull requests in 2025.
Papers
The Policies of Programming Language Ecosystems (Jukka Ruohonen et al., arXiv) codes the published policies of eight package registries against 38 categories. All eight cover malware, intellectual property and content removal, while treatment of package size limits, metric manipulation, typo-squatting and binary uploads varies.
Supply Chain Insecurity: Exposing Vulnerabilities in iOS Dependency Management Systems (David Schmidt et al., arXiv) finds that iOS apps expose internal CocoaPods package names, which attackers can then register to run code on developer machines and build servers. Across 9,212 apps, hijacking a single CocoaPod through an abandoned domain could have compromised 63 of them.
Elsewhere
The call for participation for the Package Management devroom at FOSDEM 2027 is open until 1 December. I’m co-organising with Vlad Miricioiu, Wolf Vollprecht and Travis Hathaway. The Ruby devroom is also back for the first time in several years.
EasyBuild has joined the High Performance Software Foundation at the Core stage, the highest of HPSF’s three project stages.
Michał Górny’s The next circle of security hell is a follow-up to his 2021 “modern packager’s security nightmare” post, on vulnerability report volume and projects that bundle security fixes with feature and API changes.
Josh Bressers wrote up curl’s new policy of handling low and medium severity reports in public, covered here last week, and argues other projects should adopt it.
git-pkgs
I tagged 6 repos this week:
purl2swhid v0.1.0 (new), which turns a Package URL into a Software Heritage identifier and can request archival through Save Code Now
skills v0.2.0 (new), a Go library for finding and parsing Agent Skills in checkouts and package archives
typosquatting v0.1.0 (new), a Go library that generates package-name variants and checks names against a supplied corpus for PyPI, npm, RubyGems, Cargo, Go and GitHub Actions
enrichment v0.7.5
purl v0.2.1
registries v0.13.0
Send links for next week to @andrewnez@mastodon.social.

articles.title: ★ MacBook Pro Pricing and Configurations for M6, M5 Pro, and M5 Max
articles.summary:
Apple’s dynamic configuration UI in their online store doesn’t hide or disguise the pricing or configuration options, but it doesn’t present all of the options at a glance. I find it useful to organize all of the configuration options into tables on a single page, and I figured it might be useful to share this now, before I finish writing my full thoughts on the redesigned hardware and displays for the PROLED XDR models.
Notes:
The old-style (mini-LED, no touchscreens, heavier) M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pros were announced and began shipping in March 2026, alongside the new Studio Display and Studio Display XDR, the MacBook Neo, and M5 MacBook Airs.


The new but old-style plain 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro was announced in October 2026 and is set to begin shipping in early November.


The all-new PROLED XDR (touchscreens, lighter weight) M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pros were announced in October 2026 and are set to begin shipping in early November.


As in previous generations, there are no 16-inch models for the plain M6 or the chip-binned fewer-core M5 Pro configurations. The 16-inch MacBook Pro starts with the full 18-core CPU / 20-core GPU M5 Pro chip.


16-inch models, when available, cost $300 more than the same-specced 14-inch configuration.


Nano-texture displays are an option for all MacBook Pro models, and always cost $150.


The new PROLED XDR models cost $400 more than the equivalent old-style ones. This $400 difference is true for both 14- and 16-inch models.


The new 16 TB SSD upgrade is exclusively available for M5 Max models with the new PROLED XDR displays. It costs a smooth $7,000 more than the base 2 TB storage.

    16-inch:          N/A

To me, the most curious detail in these tables is that if you select the chip-binned M5 Max with only 32 GPU cores, the one and only RAM configuration is 36 GB. The “full” M5 Max with 40 GPU cores starts with 48 GB of RAM in the base configuration.
For size, weight, battery life, and display brightness differences, consult Apple’s ever-excellent Compare tool, preconfigured with that link to show the 14-inch models with M6, M5 Max (mini-LED), and M5 Max with PROLED XDR. (PDF archive of that Compare page, archived today for posterity.)

articles.title: College will only cost $20 a month
articles.summary:
From 2020 to 2022, I've encouraged a steady stream of students to pursue their education in computer science. Tech companies were hiring like crazy. I would interview 3 candidates a week on some occasions. The future of tech seemed to be paved with gold. Any day now, several of those students will graduate. I dread opening my inbox and get an email from them asking:
			
"So... about those jobs?"
Things have changed since those crazy old days. Hiring has come to a stop. Those graduates will step into a market that looks nothing like what they signed up for. Getting a job will be a struggle. If I could see the future, I would have recommended a different path. But then again, how could I have known? Hindsight is always 20/20.
So this leaves me with a dilemma as a parent. What do I tell my own kids? Am I going to push them to pursue the same traditional colleges? Will I disburse life savings so they could attend a prestigious university? Or will I just buy them a $20 a month AI Subscription?
Imagine handing a student a textbook straight from a university syllabus. They read a lesson, and then you have an AI tutor to quiz them, debate concepts, and break down difficult ideas until they fully grasp the material. Is that a good replacement for college?
Some argue that college is about the experience. It's the friendships you make along the way, the networking, the independence. These same people often omit the lifetime of crippling debt that hangs over those friends twenty years later.
When I was in college, I focused almost entirely on mastering the material in the books, completing all assignments quickly. I spent the rest of the semesters tutoring my peers and applying the material I had learned. For me replacing the entire college system, the brick-and-mortar university with a set of books and an AI subscription seems like it would have done the job. I was the target candidate for this model.
Yet, now that I have these AIs to experiment it myself, I found two flaws in the model:
Understanding takes time.
Not having an immediate answer forces you to strain your brain until you figure things out.
When I wrestled with dense textbooks in college, solutions didn't arrive at the click of a button. Instead, I struggled. I hit dead ends. I tried solutions that seemed promising only to abruptly stop two hours in the process only to realize that the whole thing was wrong. Sitting with the problem, the trials, the errors, giving up and going for a walk to clear my head, that was the process that taught me how to think. It taught me how to debug.
Even when I found solutions online and pasted them into my code, I had to encounter the same problem repeatedly before the concept finally made sense. You have to work your way through a solution to understand a problem.
This is why I feel concerned when we throw Millennium Prize Mathematical problems at AI. Imagine an AI presents a complete proof to one of these unsolved problems tomorrow? If or when AI solves it, we still have two problems. 
We still have to understand the solution. Having an AI produce a proof doesn't mean we understand how or why it works.
We don't get to discover new problems. 
The second one is often overlooked, but ask yourself, where do these problems in Mathematics come from? They come from mathematicians attempting to solve hard problems, taking detours and failing along the way. Remove that step, and you... Well, you don't find any new problems.
Not just in mathematics, I feel we will see something similar in code where fewer applications rely on frameworks. Frameworks solve real issues in programming, but why use a framework when the AI can just give you all the answers. I lived through the JS framework mania. I am not suggesting we create more, but I think we will miss out on discovering new problems that need solving.
If we rely on a system that just hands us a solution, we lose the ability to uncover new questions because we never went through the steps of trying something new.
I don't think a $20-a-month AI subscription paired with a textbook is the ultimate solution. Not when we still need some friction in order to inculcate concepts in our minds. But traditional higher education has changed so drastically and the skyrocketing costs and changing employment realities don’t help. There is no turning back to the old model either.
The challenge for learning remains understanding. How we grasp concepts and develop critical thinking in an era of instant answers. Maybe that's where we should turn our focus to. Figuring out how to design learning that somehow preserves productive struggle. If AI can solve this issue and turn students into masters of crafts instead of prompt engineers, I mean, I'll gladly keep that college tuition in my pocket.

articles.summary:
Happy Halloween! Here’s a little of what I got up to in this spooky month.
Things I did in October
I moved this site from an Apache-powered VPS to CDN-frontend object storage. This means I pay less money, I do less maintenance, and my site loads faster in most parts of the world. Hopefully nobody noticed this change, except that things should be a little snappier! (Also, my old site had a small amount of PHP, which I’m happy to have removed given PHP’s remote code execution vulnerabilities this month.)
In an effort to fill in the gaps of the internet, I published a short list of Vim forks.
At Ghost, my team shipped two additions to our automations feature: analytics and more granular triggers. Both of these should help our independent publishers grow. More automations stuff on the way!
Like every month, I wrote a few articles at Zelda Dungeon, including a debate over, perhaps, the most trivial disagreement possible.
Tech links I clicked on
The surveillance state takes another step: pinpointing addresses based on interior photos. Thanks, AI!
“How Technology Empowers—and Imperils—Dictators” is a reminder that technologists have a social duty.
Two lists of tech fascists: “Fashware” and “Weird little guys of FOSS”.
Continued to love David Rosenthal’s blog about the (seemingly unsustainable) economics of AI companies.
“Keyboard differences between Windows and Macs” is a deep dive into Control and Command and Copilot keys.
Data centers are unpopular, a problem Amazon is trying to spend its way out of.
“Programming Isn’t Special” argues that programming is art, and that most art isn’t “mystical”, and that using AI to do art has disadvantages. “If we use AI to erase all the copy-writing, all the graphic design, all the boring mundane art, and yes, all the boring custom WordPress theme development, then we will be removing all the practical opportunities for the vast amounts of practice and contemplation required for people to elevate their craft to eventually achieve great things.”
A fun AGENTS.md that says, “All LLM contributions are strictly forbidden.”
Other miscellany
Part biography, part memoir, part hopeful, part depressing…Why Fish Don’t Exist captivated me this month.
I plan to consult The Ultimate List of DRM-free Bookshops next time I buy an ebook.
Bookmarked this list of “every weird film ever (with a special emphasis on trash)”.
As a lifelong Diddy Kong Racing fan, I felt personally insulted by “Bloke Who Preferred The Thinking Man’s Mario Kart Growing Up Also A Weird Contrarian In Other Aspects Of His Strange Life”.
Hope you had a good October.

articles.summary: Today's links Formalities: When it comes to AI, the Copyright Office is restoring copyright to its proper status, as something you have to work to get. Formalities (permalink) It's not often that I find myself on the same side as the US Copyright Office. In fact, I think this is the first time in 25 years that I've found myself cheering on the office's official actions as good for art and good for free expression, taking the side of creative workers over our bosses. The source of our miraculous accord: the US Copyright Office's position on AI. The CO has taken the (entirely correct) position that copyright law exists to incentivize human acts of creative expression, which means that only works of human authorship are eligible for copyright. This isn't a controversial position within legal circles. But for media executives, this is shocking; absurd, even. This gap between the industrial and the legal understanding of copyright comes from a fundamental difference over the evocatively named legal doctrine of "sweat of the brow." "Sweat of the brow" is fundamental to a correct legal understanding of copyright. Copyright rewards and protects creativity but it does not protect hard work. You can labor for ten years over a phone book listing the numbers of every person in a town and (as a collection of uncopyrightable facts) it will receive no protection at all. Zero. Zilch. Anyone can copy and sell that phone book: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feist_Publications,_Inc._v._Rural_Telephone_Service_Co. Copyright law doesn't care if you slaved over that collection of facts, if you missed sleep and your kids' little league games to realize your grand vision. Copyright law doesn't care if you plowed every cent into it, remortgaging your home and cashing in your (already resentful) kids' college funds. But: if you dash off a haiku in ten seconds while sitting on the toilet, shove it into your pocket and forget about it, and then your (still resentful) kids discover that crumpled haiku after your (highly suspicious) death, your kids will be able to claim a full 70 years' worth of copyright over that forgotten triviality (the term of copyright for works of human authorship is life plus 70 years). This is the uncontroversial and universally accepted legal understanding of copyright: all the copyright in the world for creative acts, no copyright at all for mere acts of labor. The "sweat of the brow" has nothing to do with a work's eligibility for copyright. But no media boss believes this. For media bosses, copyright is a pseudo-property† right, designed and operated to protect their bottom line. The point of copyright isn't to incentivize creativity, but rather investment. † Or not-so-pseudo There's obviously a relationship between creative acts and acts of investment, but it's possible to create without investment (see: your haiku) and it's possible to invest without creativity (see: your phone book). And once again, the creativity that copyright protects is human creativity. This is a lesson that David Slater learned the hard way. Slater is a professional wildlife photographer and amateur monkey-trainer who combined his interests by teaching Celebes crested macaque monkeys to take selfies. But when Slater published a monkey's selfie others copied and distributed the image without his permission, on the (entirely legally correct) basis that monkeys are not humans, and that means that works created by monkeys don't get a copyright. This was also the Copyright Office's position, and the position of the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monkey_selfie_copyright_dispute This is the basis for the US Copyright Office's repeated decision to refuse to extend copyright to AI-generated works. An algorithm is even less human than a monkey, so if you can't get copyright over a monkey selfie, you definitely can't copyright your chatbot's slop. The US Copyright Office has successfully defended this position in multiple courts, triumphing over plaintiffs who were so persistent that they even got the Supreme Court to weigh in on the issue (the Supremes decided the case didn't warrant their attention): https://pluralistic.net/2026/03/03/its-a-trap-2/#inheres-at-the-moment-of-fixation AI slop isn't copyrightable, but there can be copyrightable elements in an AI-generated image. The most obvious element is the prompt. So long as your prompt contains some quantum of creativity (e.g. "Make me a beautiful flower whose loveliness is reminiscent of a newborn baby", but not "make me a beautiful flower"), that prompt is copyrightable. That means you can use copyright to challenge others' rights to present the same prompt to a chatbot. But while the prompt can be copyrighted, the image it gives rise to isn't. So you can spend a month iteratively refining your prompt, consuming all your town's water along with 200,000 gallons of diesel and that prompt will be yours for your life plus 70 years, but the image it generates is in the public domain, and anyone can copy it, sell it or give it away. There are other ways that copyright can find its way into AI-generated material. You can make creative edits to it: if you output a slop novel and rewrite various sentences (providing those rewrites involve some creativity and not just mechanical corrections or word substitutions), then the edited sentences become copyrighted works, even though all the rest of the text remains uncopyrightable. You can also get a "thin" copyright through selection. If you get your chatbot to output many images based on your prompt and choose your favorite, your selection can confer a tiny bit of copyright over that creative act of selection, but it will be harder to defend than even the other (attenuated and highly specific) forms of copyright. Now, perhaps you've spotted an administrative problem lurking in this turn of events. How can someone else know what part of a work is AI-generated (and thus in the public domain) and which parts are human-edited/contributed (and thus copyrighted)? Just as importantly, how can you prove which parts of your work are not AI-generated and thus eligible for copyright protection. This gets especially gnarly when you're dealing with complex media. In an animation, an AI might do the rigging and movement for a human-created sprite. The sprite is copyrightable, but its movements aren't. That would mean that I could remap your sprite's movements onto a different sprite without infringing your copyright. Or say the sprite and its movements are human created (and thus copyrighted), but the backgrounds are procedurally generated? I could take those backgrounds and put new animations overtop of them. The simplest, most reliable way to ensure the works you invest in are fully and entirely eligible for copyright is to just use humans for the whole project. Declare a "no-AI policy," and hire human artists to produce the works you hope to sell. Monitor their activity to ensure they're not using AI. Keep good records. Now, as much as I like the idea that we've arrived at a copyright law that insists that a company can only get exclusive rights to its products by paying human artists to make them from end-to-end, I don't think that's likely to be the way it shakes out, but that doesn't mean that this is a wash for artists. The reality is that copyright claims are always "fact-intensive inquiries" that are expensive to litigate and difficult to adjudicate. It's completely normal for copyright lawsuits to turn on documentary evidence gleaned from fragmentary records. This is simply intrinsic to copyright, because copyright is a doctrine that requires judges to assess whether things are "creative" and "original" as though these were freestanding categories that everyone could agree upon. Of course, the rules of copyright can make this harder or easier. One way in which the rules make deciding copyright cases much, much harder is copyright's broad prohibition on "formalities" ("formalities" is how copyright wonks refer to "red tape" or "paperwork"). For nearly all of American history, copyright ran on a key formality: deposit, registration and notice. To secure a copyright for a new work, an artist (or their employer) had to send a copy of that work to the Library of Congress (deposit), along with paperwork detailing the claim of authorship (who made this, what parts of it did they make) (registration) and they had to display a copyright notice that told you who held the copyright to every work that was registered (notice). Both the filing and the notice required careful attention and precision, and screwing either one up could result in your losing your copyright. It's an open secret among copyright scholars that Walt Disney screwed this up with the first Mickey cartoons, meaning they've been in the public domain since their release: https://web.archive.org/web/20080725055415/http:/homepages.law.asu.edu/~dkarjala/opposingcopyrightextension/publicdomain/HedenkampFreeMickeyMouseVaSp&E(2003).htm This system of copyright formalities meant that you could always tell whether a work was copyrighted, you could always find out who claimed the copyright over it, and which parts of the work were claimed under copyright and under what basis. What's more, formalities created the Library of Congress, since the LoC acted as America's "copyright deposit" library, holding deposit copies of every work that had ever been issued a US copyright. The US system of formalities was descended from the English system, in which the Stationers' Guild used a copyright registry to establish who had the rights to which books. But there were competing copyright systems, notably the "continental" system that was codified through the Berne Convention, a copyright treaty drafted by Victor Hugo (yes, that Victor Hugo). Among other things, the Berne Convention abolished formalities. Much of the world adopted Berne, but the US held out until 1976. With the 1976 Copyright Act, Congress brought the US into compliance with Berne, abolishing formalities in the USA. As a compromise, the 1976 Act requires US authors to register their copyrights in order to obtain "statutory damages" (up to $150,000 per work). That's a pretty good incentive, but even with that incentive, the vast majority – far in excess of 99.999999999999999999999999999999999999999% – of all copyrighted works are not registered with the Copyright Office. They are born copyrighted from the moment they are "fixed in a tangible medium" until 70 years after their authors die. But without registration, you can't know when that copyright clock started ticking because you have no way to verify who the author of the work is. This not only makes it incredibly difficult to establish the copyright status of nearly every copyrighted work, but it also means that in nearly every case, you can't readily determine who you should approach if you want to pay them for a copyright license. Abolishing formalities has created a universe of orphan works: everything from napkin doodles to kindergartners' finger paintings to message board posts. Within that universe is a kind of gaseous cloud that, if condensed, would come out to an infinitesimal planetoid, representing the entirety of commercial works whose authors give a damn about their copyright status. It's a bad, bad system. This system doesn't do away with the need to keep careful records: like I said, copyright disputes usually require the close examination of documentary evidence. What formality abolition accomplished was the destruction of the regular system of record-keeping: rather than having a standard, universally agreed-upon way to determine the status and resolve disputes about a copyrighted work, now we have the scattershot, incoherent system that makes copyright disputes far more likely (because no one knows who to approach for copyright licenses) and far more difficult to resolve (because there's no registry of copyrighted works). Which brings me back to the question of AI and copyright. If a firm uses some AI in its work, it's going to need to document that very carefully. Firms that don't keep very close track of the elements of their products that come from AI will have a far harder time defending their commercial interests. Basically, we're about to recreate formalities, but managed by the private sector. To the extent that companies use AI in their work, they are going to have to track every pixel and every word and every note that is output by an AI system, and which parts were added or edited by humans after creation. That means that companies that want to protect their commercial interests aren't just going to get more protection based on how much work they get humans to do; they're also going to have to treat copyright's government-enforceable monopoly over expressive speech with the gravitas it deserves: not something you get automatically, but something you have to do real administrative work for. articles.title: Sponsorship Openings for Daring Fireball (Including The Talk Show)
articles.summary:
Sponsorships have continued selling briskly, of late. Knock on wood. As of yesterday, the next opening on the schedule wasn’t until the last week of December, and the Q1 2027 schedule is already filling up. However, due to some schedule rejiggering, next week is now open. Update: OK, next week has been sold, but Christmas week remains open. That’s a good week at DF. I keep posting and readers are often more bored than usual. Also a good week to promote games.
If you’ve got a product or service you think would be of interest to DF’s audience of people obsessed with high quality and good design, just email me — especially if you can act quick for next week’s opening. I’m also booking sponsorships for Q1 and Q2 2027, and over half of those weeks are already sold. The rate for the two remaining weeks in 2026 is $11,000, and the rate for open weeks in 2027 is $12,500.
The sponsorship schedule for The Talk Show also has openings, including for the next few episodes in November and December. The general rule of thumb is that sponsorship spots on The Talk Show cost one-third the rate for the weekly spots on DF. I’m happy to work out deals a little lower than that for first-time sponsors. If you’ve got a product or service you’d like to hear pitched on America’s favorite three-star podcast, get in touch.
